feedback: If a learner says the largest sperm wins, redirect to: fertilisation is a single sperm penetrating the egg, and size is not the deciding factor.
If a learner thinks many eggs are released each cycle, clarify that usually one egg is released.
activities.intendedInsight: The two gametes have complementary structures matched to their roles; fertilisation is one sperm joining one egg, not a size contest.
learnerActions: Compare sperm and egg side by side: describe sperm as small, numerous and motile, and the egg as large and food-storing.
Explain why these complementary features suit each gamete's role in fertilisation.
Correct the idea that the 'biggest/strongest' sperm wins by size — fertilisation is a single sperm penetrating one egg; usually one egg is released per cycle.
activities.title: Contrast the two gametes

feedback: Keep explanations at the level of lining build-up, egg release and shedding; if a learner asks about hormones, acknowledge that is studied later and keep the current model at the required boundary.
activities.intendedInsight: The menstrual cycle is a monthly preparation of the uterus and release of an egg; at this stage it is understood without hormonal detail.
learnerActions: Use a simple cycle calendar to describe the monthly pattern: the uterus lining builds up, an egg is released, and the lining is shed if no fertilisation occurs.
Describe the cycle's purpose (preparing the uterus lining and releasing an egg) without naming hormones.
activities.title: The menstrual cycle without hormones

feedback: Keep the scope to vetted factual questions; model a calm clinical register and reinforce that questions are safe to ask.
activities.intendedInsight: Sensitive factual questions can be asked and answered safely in an appropriate professional register.
learnerActions: In a safe, ground-ruled space, write factual questions about reproduction to put to a trusted professional voice (e.g. a school nurse or midwife persona), coordinated with RSE and safeguarding.
Use answers to resolve genuine uncertainties in a calm, respectful register.
activities.title: Ask a professional — vetted factual questions (supplement)

feedback: Full response: explains the placenta as a two-way exchange surface where oxygen, nutrients and waste pass (mainly by diffusion) between the mother's and baby's SEPARATE supplies, with the umbilical cord carrying the baby's blood to and from the placenta, locates development in the uterus and fertilisation (gamete fusion) in the oviduct, and links maternal lifestyle to foetal development.

Partial: knows the placenta feeds the baby and can name the gametes as separate facts but cannot explain diffusion across two separate blood supplies, or misplaces fertilisation — prompt with 'how do oxygen and food actually get across if the bloods don't mix?'.
Gap: says the baby is in the stomach or that the bloods mix — reteach the uterus location and the separate-supplies/diffusion model.
Probe further: 'Why can alcohol or nicotine still affect the baby if the blood doesn't mix?' and 'What is the umbilical cord's job?'
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can both recall the structures/sequence and explain, in their own words, the placenta's two-way exchange between separate blood supplies.
learnerActions: Match each organ to its function (organ to function).
Put the stages in order: egg release → fertilisation → implantation → birth.
Answer where fertilisation occurs, and select which substances can cross the placenta.

Answer the two-tier diagnostic in your own words: 'During pregnancy, how does a growing baby get its oxygen and food, and get rid of its waste, while inside the mother? Explain the placenta's job — and does the mother's blood flow straight into the baby?'
activities.title: Check your understanding
